subject: AI & Agents
title: The Productivity Paradox: More AI, Same Growth?
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Productivity Paradox: More AI, Same Growth? usable.

hook.text: We have the most powerful AI in history, yet economic productivity growth remains stubbornly slow.

buildup.text: The same paradox happened with computers in the 1980s — Nobel economist Solow noted it first.

discovery.text: New technologies take decades to reshape workflows, organizations, and skills before productivity surges.

twist.text: Electricity took 30 years to boost factory output. AI adoption may follow a similar slow curve.

climax.text: The productivity gains from AI may be enormous — but they're coming later than the hype suggests.

punchline.text: Revolutionary technology, evolutionary adoption. Patience, humanity.

quiz.question: Why haven't AI productivity gains appeared immediately in economic data?
options: New technologies take decades to reshape workflows and organizations

details.summary: Despite billions invested in AI, overall economic productivity has not surged as expected. This productivity paradox echoes similar delays seen with electricity and computers before AI.
details.whyItMatters: The paradox challenges AI hype by showing that technology alone does not drive growth. Organizational transformation and human adaptation are equally essential for AI to deliver returns.
takeaways: AI investment has not yet produced proportional productivity gains
Similar paradoxes occurred with electricity and early computing
Organizational change is needed to unlock AI's economic potential

faq.question: Why hasn't AI dramatically increased productivity yet?
faq.answer: Transformative technologies need complementary innovations in workflows, skills, and organizational structure. These changes take years to decades, lagging behind the technology itself.

faq.question: Did past technologies show the same productivity delay?
faq.answer: Yes. Electric motors took 30 years to transform factories because buildings and workflows needed redesigning. Computers showed a similar lag before productivity benefits appeared in the 1990s.
